title: Trees and Hash Tables: Concepts
description: A conceptual introduction to binary trees and hash tables, and how they'd be represented in C.
objectives: Understand the conceptual structure of a binary tree in C
Understand the conceptual structure and purpose of a hash table

content.heading: Binary Trees
content.body: A binary tree node, like a linked list node, is a struct — but with (up to) two pointers to child nodes instead of one 'next' pointer: struct TreeNode { int data; struct TreeNode *left; struct TreeNode *right; };. A binary search tree (BST) additionally maintains an ordering invariant: every node's left subtree contains only smaller values, and its right subtree only larger ones, which makes searching, insertion, and deletion all average O(log n) for a reasonably balanced tree (though a poorly-balanced tree, such as one built by inserting already-sorted data, degrades toward O(n), behaving like a linked list). Tree operations (insertion, traversal, search) are naturally expressed recursively, since each subtree has the exact same shape as the whole tree.

content.heading: Hash Tables
content.body:
A hash table maps keys to values with average O(1) lookup, insertion, and deletion — dramatically faster than a linear search through an array or list for large datasets. Conceptually, it works by applying a hash function to a key, producing an index into a fixed-size array of 'buckets'; the value (or key-value pair) is stored at that bucket. Because different keys can hash to the same bucket index (a collision), a real implementation needs a collision-resolution strategy — commonly chaining (each bucket holds a linked list of entries that hashed there) or open addressing (probing for the next free slot according to some rule).

C has no built-in hash table in its standard library (unlike Python's dict or Java's HashMap) — implementing one yourself (or using a well-tested third-party library) requires writing the hash function, the bucket array, and the collision-resolution logic explicitly, which is a genuinely instructive exercise in understanding what higher-level languages' built-in dictionary/map types are actually doing underneath.

content.explanation: insert() recursively descends left or right based on the BST ordering invariant. inorder() recursively visits left, then the node, then right — which, for a valid BST, always visits values in ascending sorted order.

keyPoints: A binary tree node holds data plus left/right child pointers; a BST maintains a left-smaller/right-larger ordering invariant
BST operations average O(log n) on a balanced tree but can degrade toward O(n) if poorly balanced
A hash table maps a hash function's output to bucket indices for average O(1) access
C has no built-in hash table — implementing one requires writing the hash function and collision resolution yourself
commonMistakes: Inserting already-sorted data into a plain BST, producing a degenerate, linked-list-like (unbalanced) tree
Forgetting to handle hash collisions when implementing a hash table from scratch
Leaking tree/list nodes by losing a pointer to a subtree without freeing it first
